finding.claim: The recovery CLI does not specify an immutable binding to the inspected attempt, allowing a delayed or repeated recovery invocation to apply an old operator assertion to a newer uncertain attempt.

finding.evidence:
[artifact.md:53,79,81,85; root spec CLI and compatibility and Human recovery; recovery task ht-qhz.6] The documented commands are human handoff recover REF --created-pane EXACT_PANE or --not-created (line 53), while recovery is required to reference an exact attempt (line 79), and not-created enables a distinct next attempt (line 81). The spec never defines REF as an immutable attempt-qualified recovery reference or exposes an expected-attempt parameter. A ready command retained while attempt A is uncertain can therefore be executed after another operator closes A and retry creates uncertain attempt B: resolving the same bootstrap REF to its current attempt applies an assertion based on inspection of A to B. Per-attempt deterministic keys and canonical contradictory-decision checks do not reject that newly selected B decision. The contract needs an immutable inspected-attempt reference in generated/user-facing recovery commands and stale-attempt refusal; the full recovery task specifies exact attempt references internally but no such user-to-attempt binding.

[artifact.md:53, 79–81 (recovery CLI and exact-attempt recovery/replay contract)] The only recovery grammar is `human handoff recover REF --created-pane EXACT_PANE` or `--not-created`; no expected-attempt argument or attempt-qualified REF semantics are defined. The canonical contract nevertheless says recovery references the "exact attempt", that not-created enables "a distinct next attempt", and that "Replaying either recovery key is presentation only". If an operator inspects attempt A, another recovery closes A, and a retry makes attempt B uncertain before the delayed command executes, resolving the bootstrap REF to the current attempt applies the old inspection assertion to B. Deterministic per-attempt mutation keys do not prevent this because choosing B produces a different key. The interface must define how the user-visible recovery invocation freezes A before the deciding transaction; neither the nested specs nor recovery task ht-qhz.6 supplies that binding.

Mutation keys are children of compound and phase/attempt (line 63); recovery references an exact attempt and replaying its key must be presentation only, while not-created enables a distinct next attempt (line 81). Consider a committed not-created decision whose reply is lost, then an original-agent retry that reaches possible_creation on the next attempt, then a retry of the operator command. The design does not define a durable recovery invocation journal/key, expected-attempt precondition exposed to the operator, or other binding that prevents resolving REF to the newer attempt and treating the old inspection assertion as a new decision. Consider successful --not-created for attempt A, retry creating uncertain attempt B, then re-execution of the previously emitted --not-created command for A: selecting the current attempt B applies an inspection assertion to the wrong attempt, while always selecting A makes the displayed syntax insufficient to recover B. If --not-created for attempt A commits but its reply is lost, an original-agent retry can reserve attempt B before the operator repeats the same displayed recovery command. Resolving the compound REF to the latest attempt then constructs a new B recovery key, so key-level idempotency does not preserve the operator's original assertion about A. The design needs to specify the mechanism tying the inspection and recovery command to A across response loss; listing attempt IDs in reports (line 85) and retaining exact decisions alone does not define that mechanism.

votes.evidence: Internal design gap; no external premise is needed. The whole root/nested/task bundle was read. The missing boundary is user invocation to inspected attempt: artifact.md:53 gives recover REF with only a decision/pane selector, while :79 requires an exact attempt and :85 promises ready guarded recovery argv preserving attempt information. Neither those sections, the inherited nested specs, nor ht-qhz.6 defines REF as attempt-qualified or supplies an expected-attempt/invocation identity. Concrete sequence: (1) reserve attempt A and lose its reply/result; :69 and :71 leave A possible_creation/outcome_unknown and require recovery guidance. The operator inspects A and retains the displayed --not-created invocation. (2) A valid recovery records no effect and permits a distinct next attempt (:81); its response can be lost, or another operator can make that decision. (3) ordinary agent retry reserves B under the same immutable bootstrap, then B also becomes uncertain (:69, :71, :81). Both invocations have ended, so the known-in-flight lock refusal in :81 does not stop the scenario. (4) repeating the retained command has no specified input distinguishing replay of the assertion about A from a fresh assertion about B. If dispatch selects current B and derives B's deterministic recovery child key (:63), its canonical decision is individually unique and noncontradictory, yet closes B using inspection of A. This breaks the intended exact-attempt assertion binding (:79, :81) and the presentation-only recovery replay requirement (:81); an ensuing retry can create again without any inspected noncreation assertion for B. Always selecting A instead prevents this replay error but leaves the documented command unable to address B unless REF semantics are extended. The accepted limit (:83) permits an operator's mistaken noncreation/quiescence assertion; it does not accept silently moving a correct A assertion onto B. An attempt-qualified REF could solve this within the displayed grammar, but defining and requiring that binding in emitted argv is precisely the omitted contract, rather than an existing mitigation.

(a) Present under another name: the complete artifact requires an 'exact attempt' in Human recovery and ht-qhz.6, deterministic phase/attempt mutation keys, retained decisions, reports containing attempts, normal-operation-lock refusal, and presentation-only recovery-key replay. (c) Scope: binding the documented recovery invocation to its intended attempt is part of the specified recovery/replay surface, not adversarial verification, native idempotency, or stronger distributed atomicity. The installer-lane signature gate defers concrete integration but supplies no binding contract in this artifact. (d) Materiality: A's not-created decision can commit with its response lost; an agent retry then reserves B and also becomes uncertain; repeating the identical recovery command can select B and close it based on inspection of A. Once neither invocation holds the operation lock, the stated quiescence guard does not distinguish this stale assertion. A further retry can submit another tab despite B possibly having created one. Per-attempt decisions and late-success conflict detection cannot prevent that extra creation. This is a significant recovery correctness risk requiring a frozen operator-visible attempt reference or an equivalent durable invocation binding and stale-attempt handling. Line 53 supplies only recover REF plus the decision; it does not define REF as an immutable attempt reference. Lines 79 and 935 require exact attempt references, while line 81 permits a distinct next attempt and promises recovery-key replay is presentation only. This is a real interface specification gap in the stated conservative replay contract, rather than a demand to prevent the explicitly accepted mistaken operator assertion. Define an attempt-qualified recovery REF or explicit expected-attempt input, emit it in recovery guidance, and retain replay/refusal semantics for that exact attempt. No external premise is needed.

finding.claim: The design does not specify how to reconcile a downstream-complete but bootstrap-incomplete crash when caller or topology guards become invalid before retry, potentially stranding the live outer fence.

finding.evidence:
[artifact.md:73,75 and bootstrap-coordinator section Downstream launch and terminal bootstrap replay (lines 177–183)] The downstream handoff has its own canonical completion, and only afterward can the bootstrap complete with validated retained presentation (line 75). These are separate named Complete commands and no atomic cross-completion transaction is specified. Retry ordinarily revalidates exact topology, incarnation and guarded seat mapping and refuses missing panes or changed incarnation (line 73); the explicit bypass and zero-effect retained presentation guarantee applies to a completed bootstrap (line 75 and line 183). A crash after downstream completion but before CompleteBootstrap therefore leaves an outer live fence even though all work is already terminal. If the host restarts or recipient binding changes before retry, the text does not require checking the attached downstream terminal state before those live guards, nor authorize finishing only the outer canonical bookkeeping from that retained result. The downstream-complete/outer-live intermediate state needs an explicit recovery branch and failure test; tests for an already completed bootstrap do not cover it.

[artifact.md, root spec “Topology state machine and response loss”, paragraphs beginning “The result records” and “After attachment”; nested bootstrap coordinator “Downstream launch and terminal bootstrap replay”; ht-qhz.4.3 and ht-qhz.2.3.] The root requires “Current host reads and canonical ordinary guarded seat resolution must still confirm that exact topology, same incarnation and mapping” and refuses missing panes/incarnation changes. Therefore downstream Complete can commit, the coordinator can crash before CompleteBootstrap, and the pane or original caller binding can change before retry. The downstream is terminal but the bootstrap is still live. The combined contract specifies neither atomic completion of both fences nor an early downstream-terminal reconciliation path that can validate the retained result and complete the bootstrap without re-running live caller/topology/resolution guards. Existing completed-bootstrap tests do not specify this intermediate two-fence state. The missing transition can strand an already-finished handoff behind live bootstrap archival protection.
